channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Exercise can sometimes cause chest pain—and this condition may be to blame
item.description: As a general practitioner, I know that chest pain is one symptom that makes people worry. The immediate concern is that it's a sign there's something seriously wrong—such as a problem with their heart or lungs.

item.title: Analysis of 244 million Americans refines the understanding of long COVID
item.description: Long COVID is a phenomenon in which serious health effects linger well after a patient tests negative for coronavirus infection. Patients describe persistent "brain fog," fatigue, dizziness, rapid heart rate, shortness of breath and chest pain, among symptoms that affect nearly every organ system in the body and last a year or more after the infection has passed.

item.title: Unifying mechanism explains how common cancer mutations fuel growth
item.description: A family of mutations seen in about 20% of human cancers drives malignancy by changing the accessibility of genes to a particular regulatory protein, according to a study by Weill Cornell Medicine investigators. The findings suggest new therapeutic strategies for a variety of cancer types.

item.title: How the heart's unusual carbohydrate metabolism helps it stay strong
item.description: The heart is the hardest-working muscle in the body, beating constantly no matter what the body's energy reserves look like. Maintaining energy flow to the heart is a complex process that can break down during common but severe cardiovascular disease conditions like heart failure. Researchers previously knew that heart muscle seems to do an unusual metabolic trick to always get enough energy: using two carbohydrate energy sources, glucose and lactate, at the same time. In most human tissues, using more glucose makes it harder to use lactate, and vice versa, but the heart is different.

item.title: Who uses nicotine pouches?
item.description: A national survey study conducted by the University of Cincinnati found that nicotine pouch use increased sharply in the United States between 2021 and 2024 among adult tobacco users.

item.title: Brain scans challenge link between prefrontal activity and ability to regulate emotions
item.description: A person's capacity to regulate their emotions apparently cannot be determined by the activity of the prefrontal brain regions typically associated with this process. This is shown by an international fMRI analysis conducted by Dr. Maurizio Sicorello of the Central Institute for Mental Health (CIMH) and Prof. Dr. Carmen Morawetz of the University of Innsbruck, using data from 2,175 people across 40 studies. The study, published in Nature, challenges widespread assumptions about the neural basis of emotion regulation and highlights where task-based imaging reaches its limits when it comes to differences between individuals.

item.title: Three studies reveal the hidden layers between DNA and disease
item.description: In three studies published in Nature today, Australian researchers have made advances in our understanding of how genetic differences between people influence disease. The team from the Garvan Institute of Medical Research, in collaboration with the Murdoch Children's Research Institute, UNSW and other partners, linked genetic risk regions for 16 diseases to possible causes in specific immune cells, identifying nearly 1,500 genes that may contribute to a range of diseases. These discoveries are set to accelerate drug development and precision medicine across many diseases, ranging from cancers to immune and neurological conditions.

item.title: Abnormal neurons are surprisingly common in the developing brain
item.description: During fetal development, the human brain generates an excess of neurons, most of which are eliminated shortly before and after birth. New research from Harvard Medical School and Boston Children's Hospital suggests that this is a critical quality-control mechanism.

item.title: Global stroke burden keeps rising despite falling stroke rates
item.description: A new Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study in Neuroepidemiology looks closely at a striking contradiction in global stroke prevention: even as age-standardized stroke rates have fallen substantially over the past three decades, the number of people suffering and dying from stroke continues to rise.

item.title: Obesity in young adulthood linked to increased risk of early-onset cancer
item.description: Having obesity in your 20s and 30s could raise your risk for early-onset cancer.

item.title: Single dose of fast-acting psychedelic nasal spray shows promise for stubborn depression
item.description: One in three individuals with major depressive disorder does not get relief from standard daily antidepressant medications. The up-and-coming psychedelic therapeutics like psilocybin or LSD do show promise of quick relief, even for difficult-to-treat depression. The psychedelic effects, however, are often strong and linger for a long time, requiring patients to remain under medical supervision in a clinic for four to 12 hours.

item.title: Health care discrimination may silence diabetes conversations among Black men
item.description: Managing type 2 diabetes requires more than occasional visits to the doctor's office. Much of the work happens between appointments, making communication and support from others an important part of managing the condition.

item.title: Mindfulness-based therapy may reshape brain responses to opioid cues during addiction treatment
item.description: Mindfulness-Oriented Recovery Enhancement (MORE), a behavioral therapy used alongside medication treatment, may help people with opioid use disorder respond differently to drug-related cues and natural rewards, according to a randomized clinical trial led by researchers at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai. The findings offer insight into how MORE may reduce opioid craving and support recovery.

item.title: A new way to measure how crisis counseling skills improve
item.description: Being a good listener can sometimes involve more than just listening. It can also mean knowing when and how to say just the right thing—a conversational skill that's invaluable to a crisis counselor.

item.title: Nearly 75% of former NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023 had CTE, analysis estimates
item.description: A new study led by Boston University researchers estimates that nearly 75% of all NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023 had chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) neuropathology. CTE is a neurodegenerative disease that has been diagnosed in individuals with substantial exposure to repetitive head impacts. It can only be definitively diagnosed after death.

item.title: Can't sleep? Try this 5-pose yin yoga routine
item.description: A good night's sleep can feel elusive for many of us, courtesy of a racing mind, a mile-long to-do list and stress getting in the way. What's a tired person to do?

item.title: Arsenic drug combo resurrects 'guardian of the genome' to fight aggressive blood cancers
item.description: A combination cancer therapy that relies on the reactivation of a tumor suppressor protein to kill leukemic and other blood cancer cells has shown promise in a small pilot trial.

item.title: How the tumor environment influences bowel cancer cells' behavior and chemotherapy response
item.description: New research led by experts at the University of Nottingham has revealed how collagen in the tumor environment can alter bowel cancer cell behavior and influence inflammatory responses to chemotherapy, highlighting potential new avenues for future research into cancer treatment. The findings, published in the Journal of Experimental & Clinical Cancer Research, highlight the importance of the environment surrounding cancer cells in shaping how they behave and respond to treatment.

item.title: Cell-level analysis reveals how ovarian tumors may develop resistance to chemotherapy
item.description: High-grade serous ovarian cancer is an aggressive form of ovarian cancer, characterized in particular by high diversity among the cells that compose a given tumor. This intratumor heterogeneity is a major challenge in understanding why some tumors respond to treatments and others resist. Additionally, this diversity is not limited to genetic differences: tumor cells that have similar genetic profiles may have different functions, depending on the genes they express and their epigenetic state.

item.title: Japan's telemedicine use increased from 2020 to 2024 as age gap widened
item.description: Telemedicine came into wide use during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. However, access to and use of telemedicine may vary according to factors such as age, educational attainment, income, employment status and place of residence, though it has long been unclear whether these disparities would narrow as the use of telemedicine spread.

item.title: Researchers develop privacy-friendly, secure and sustainable AI techniques for medical imaging
item.description: Artificial intelligence can be helpful in analyzing medical images and support radiotherapy planning workflows. However, huge amounts of sensitive patient data are needed to train robust AI models. Researchers at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT) have investigated how hospitals can jointly develop AI models for radiation therapy applications without exchanging such data. In their project, they use federated learning, a process in which a single model is trained at a decentralized location while the data remains in place. Their results demonstrate not only the technical feasibility of the approach but also its safe, more sustainable, and accessible use.

item.title: How a neurologist is rethinking stroke prevention for the longevity era
item.description: For decades, stroke prevention has revolved around a list of separate—and often separately treated—risk factors: blood pressure, cholesterol, diabetes, smoking and inactivity. According to Dr. Gustavo Saposnik, it's time to start considering biological age as a risk factor for stroke.

item.title: Running distance is associated with how female runners distribute their daily energy expenditure
item.description: Generally, total energy expenditure is expected to be higher in individuals with greater physical activity. However, the constrained total energy expenditure model suggests that greater energy expenditure during exercise may be offset by lower energy expenditure during other activities or physiological processes, thereby maintaining total energy expenditure within a relatively limited range. It is unclear whether similar patterns occur in athletes engaged in long-term endurance training.

item.title: Animal and plant proteins show different associations with testosterone levels in men
item.description: Higher animal protein intake was associated with lower blood testosterone levels, while higher plant protein intake was associated with higher levels, according to a new study from the University of Eastern Finland. The findings were published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition.

item.title: Preclinical research shows macrophages can be programmed to fight solid cancer tumors
item.description: One person dies every 50 seconds in the U.S. from cancer, and an estimated 39% of people in the country will develop cancer during their lifetime. Survival rates have improved in recent decades from innovations and combinations of treatments, including surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, immunotherapy and biotechnology. Still, some cancers resist treatment or recur.

item.title: Don't let Halloween scare your heart health
item.description: Halloween season is a time for scary tricks and sweet treats. But people with heart conditions may need to take extra precautions before participating in fright nights. Baylor College of Medicine cardiologist and electrophysiologist Dr. Mohamed Gabr explains what you need to know to keep your heart healthy during this spooky season.

item.title: Fighting cancer also means fighting against social stigma
item.description: Cancer-related discrimination arises from long-lasting cultural and institutional misconceptions, with significant impacts on every part of a person's quality of life and health—and Flinders University researchers say it requires coordinated policy, legal, institutional and public education responses for change to occur.

item.title: Improve IBD bowel checks for early cancer detection
item.description: The first U.K.-wide analysis of bowel screening for patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) has identified opportunities to improve the early detection of cancer. The study—the largest of its kind globally—found that checks performed by professionals with regular experience, more time allowed for the procedure and the use of a special dye to improve visibility were each associated with finding small growths called polyps, which may become cancer.

item.title: LSD and psilocybin push brain blood flow in opposite directions, study suggests
item.description: Psychedelics are a class of compounds that alter people's perceptions, mood and mental processes. Recent clinical studies suggest that some of these compounds, such as lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) and psilocybin, could be promising for the treatment of depression and other psychiatric disorders.

item.title: Promising AI-based approach to early detection of suicide-related behavior at emergency rooms
item.description: Researchers from the University of Johannesburg (UJ) have published a promising approach to identifying people at risk of suicide-related behavior (SRB) in the journal Scientific Reports.
